Estimate parameters by ABC with random forests

Source: R/abc.R
abc_fit.Rd

Fits one regression random forest per parameter, with the statistics as predictors, following Raynal et al. (2019) and the package abcrf. Random forests need no tolerance and no choice of statistics, cope with many correlated statistics and rank their importance. predict() gives the posterior median and a credible interval from quantile regression forests (Meinshausen 2006). Statistics with more than 5% of missing or infinite values and constant statistics are dropped, and then simulations with any missing statistic.

Usage

abc_fit(table, parameters = NULL, statistics = NULL, ntree = 500, ncores = 1)

# S3 method for class 'mc_abc_fit'
predict(object, newdata, level = 0.9, ncores = 1, ...)

abc_importance(x)

Arguments

table

An mc_abc_table from abc_table(), or a data frame with the parameters and the statistics.

parameters

Names of the parameters to estimate. By default those of table.

statistics

Names of the statistics to use. By default all the others.

ntree

Number of trees per forest.

ncores

Number of threads for the forests.

object

An mc_abc_fit.

newdata

Named numeric vector of observed statistics, as from summary_stats(), or a data frame with one observation per row.

level

Probability of the credible interval.

...

Not used.

x

An mc_abc_fit.

Value

An mc_abc_fit, a list with forests (one per parameter), training, parameters, statistics and prior.

For predict(), a data frame with observation, parameter, estimate (posterior median), low, high and mean.

Details

Check with abc_recovery() that a parameter can be recovered from simulated data before trusting its estimate from real data. A good estimate does not validate the model either.

Functions

  • predict(mc_abc_fit): Posterior median and credible interval for each observation and parameter.

  • abc_importance(): Importance of each statistic for each parameter, as the decrease in impurity scaled to sum to one.

References

Meinshausen, N. (2006). Quantile regression forests. Journal of Machine Learning Research, 7, 983–999.

Raynal, L., Marin, J.-M., Pudlo, P., Ribatet, M., Robert, C. P., & Estoup, A. (2019). ABC random forests for Bayesian parameter inference. Bioinformatics, 35, 1720–1728. doi:10.1093/bioinformatics/bty867

See also

Other inference: abc_choose(), abc_cv(), abc_diagnose(), abc_ppc(), abc_recovery(), abc_table(), fold_summarise(), observe_detection(), spatial_folds()

Examples

set.seed(1)
table <- data.frame(a = runif(300), b = runif(300))
table$s1 <- table$a + rnorm(300, 0, 0.05)
table$s2 <- table$b * table$a + rnorm(300, 0, 0.05)
fit <- abc_fit(table, parameters = c("a", "b"), ntree = 100)
predict(fit, c(s1 = 0.5, s2 = 0.2))
#>   observation parameter  estimate       low      high      mean
#> 1           1         a 0.5083821 0.3529379 0.5872987 0.5063800
#> 2           1         b 0.4057038 0.2934010 0.7191584 0.4410285
